prize_parts.citation: For the conception and construction of the IceCube cubic-kilometre neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: My opening first place stands, but I hold it with less certainty about how many colleagues will join me. IceCube is a discovery in the sense I care most about: nature supplied a clue, a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos that nobody could have deduced by thought alone, and the instrument was built in order to find it. The diffuse flux is established through several independent analysis channels, and the TXS 0506+056 coincidence in 2017-18, NGC 1068 in 2022 and the Galactic-plane result in 2023 have begun to turn it into astronomy rather than a single detection. The impact is lasting for multimessenger astrophysics and the origin of cosmic rays, and there is an existential element in seeing the universe through a particle that crosses it almost untouched. The discovery is now over a decade old, so recognition is neither premature nor late. Halzen and Karle are the two clearest leaders and the pair keeps the credit to a defensible size.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds, the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors laid the ground, and any two or three names will be contested; Yoshida is credited on the shortlist but I regard his role as less decisive, which others may dispute. Source identification is still at roughly four sigma for NGC 1068 and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is unknown, so a sceptic can say the window is open but the view through it is still blurry. Finally, support is thin: only Pearce and I ranked B012 at all, while optical lattice clocks (B007) have first-place votes from three colleagues and appear on seven ballots. A prize that only two of eight members rank cannot be sustained by my enthusiasm.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven landmark, but worries that the individual-credit story is not clean enough for three or fewer people given the size of the collaboration and the AMANDA/Baikal precursors.
responses.response: I share the concern and have the same two names, Halzen and Karle. I would add that the committee's task is to identify the discovery first and the people second. The discovery is unambiguous, and the sensible attribution test is who conceived the ice-based cubic-kilometre concept and who made the detector actually work. That points to those two. I disagree mildly that the moderate statistics on source identification are a weakness for the prize: the Nobel-worthy result is the diffuse flux, which is solid, and the sources are a bonus. We should still expect the outside experts to be asked specifically about AMANDA priority.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because they moved the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, enable tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and are mature and independently reproduced; he notes the overlap with the earlier comb and ion-trap prizes.
responses.response: I agree the science is excellent and the Katori-Ye attribution is the cleanest on our list, which is why I put it third. My reservation is about what is discovered. The clocks are a superb instrument, and the tests of varying constants and dark matter are still mostly prospective. Kroll himself raises the possibility that we wait for the redefinition of the second, and I think that is a fair instinct: the discovery content will be clearer afterwards. I would not call the overlap with 2005 and 2012 disqualifying, but it makes this an improvement of a measured quantity by seven or eight orders of magnitude rather than a new phenomenon. I accept, however, that this is the candidate that can actually get a broad majority, and I will weigh that seriously in round 2.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT first and places twisted bilayer graphene fifth, noting that the experimental story is clean but the pairing mechanism is unresolved and the field is perhaps slightly early.
responses.response: I take a different view of B005 from Eriksson. I ranked it second because the theory-then-experiment arc is exactly what I want to see: a prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, then correlated insulators and superconductivity found in the lab. An unsettled pairing mechanism does not diminish the discovery, any more than the unsettled mechanism of high-Tc cuprates reduced the 1987 prize. Where I agree with him is on credit, as Cao and the 2018 experimental team are a real worry. On B018, I cannot rank DMFT above a discovery of a new phenomenon, and I note that his own text flags the Metzner omission as a real attribution risk.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as an insider, reading it as distinct from the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling prize, but concedes that the committee may judge the field too recently honoured and that Blais versus Girvin is a hard allocation.
responses.response: I ranked B044 fifth for the same reasons he lists as uncertainties. I accept that cQED is conceptually distinct from the 2025 prize, but a second superconducting-circuit award within a year invites the charge that we are rewarding the technology behind quantum computing. The fact that Johansson himself discounts his enthusiasm as a field insider seems right to me. If the committee does want a circuit-QED prize, the three-name problem is real and I would not pretend my Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Blais choice is better than his.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first, with Hubbard simulation second, and discloses a collaboration with Keller that she would need to weigh in any recusal discussion on Ti:sapphire mode-locking (B003).
responses.response: I appreciate the early disclosure. B003 is not in my ranking at all, but the committee should note it if that candidate moves up. I also take her point on B007 that the underlying atomic physics is clean and that the magic-wavelength idea is a real conceptual step and not only engineering. That is a better argument for B007 than the one I have heard about metrology records, and it moves B007 closer to my first place than my opening ranking suggested.

uncertainties: Whether outside expert reports can resolve the AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal priority questions well enough to name two or three IceCube leaders with confidence.

Whether the evidence for individual neutrino sources (NGC 1068 at about four sigma) will be judged sufficient, or whether the committee prefers to wait for KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD or IceCube-Gen2 confirmation.

Whether the committee should accept the clearest-attribution and broadest-support option (B007) over a stronger discovery case with narrower support (B012), and whether a two-part prize is feasible within the three-person limit.
Whether Yoshida should be included in a three-person credit; I currently lean against.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My ties are to David Gross (PhD supervisor), Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, none of which touch a shortlisted candidate. I also have no known connection to the IceCube collaboration or the other credited names.
